blogs.title: Can we change an AI model’s architecture without retraining it from scratch?
blogs.author: Luca Zancato
blogs.description: “Priming” reuses pretrained Transformer weights to build models with more efficient architectures at less than 1% of the original training cost and with throughputs up to twice as high.
blogs.content: Machine learning Can we change an AI model’s architecture without retraining it from scratch? “Priming” reuses pretrained Transformer weights to build models with more efficient architectures at less than 1% of the original training cost and with throughputs up to twice as high. By Luca Zancato October 12, 2026 14 min read Share Share Copy link Email X LinkedIn Facebook Line Reddit QZone Sina Weibo WeChat WhatsApp 分享到微信 x Key takeaways A new AWS paper introduces priming, a method that reduces pretraining costs for hybrid architectures by over 99% by leveraging pretrained Transformer weights, saving trillions of tokens and hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours. A 32-billion-parameter Gated KalmaNet (GKA)-based hybrid model matches its source Transformer on reasoning benchmarks while decoding up to twice as quickly with 128,000 tokens of context. State space models consistently outperform sliding-window attention (SWS) even when SWA receives twice the memory budget, and GKA's variable-iteration mechanism enables 10% faster decoding with only ~1% accuracy loss. Was this answer helpful? AI agents are rapidly scaling: longer sessions, deeper reasoning chains, more autonomy. But the Transformer architecture underneath them still pays a memory tax that grows with the number of tokens it processes. As agents become more capable, that cost scales with them. Now, there’s a proliferation of hybrid architectures that use some combination of methods to achieve a better balance of memory, speed, and quality. Those methods include sparse attention, which selects a subset of past tokens to consider when selecting the next token; sliding-window attention, which preserves only the most recent tokens; and state space models, which compress information from the full history into a fixed-size state. These hybrid architectures can be understood as points in a sequence-model design space: to differing degrees, they mix information while traversing a sequence and passing through different states. What distinguishes them from each other is how they retain and use the past. Until now, exploring this design space has required training every new architecture from scratch, using trillions of tokens and hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours. This has made controlled comparisons of hybrid architectures extremely expensive. In a new paper, “ Priming: Hybrid state space models from pre-trained Transformers ,” our team at Amazon Web Services addresses this problem. We introduce priming, a method that leverages pretrained Transformer weights as a starting point to reduce the pretraining cost of hybrid architectures by more than 99%. With priming, model developers can ask questions that were previously too expensive to answer at scale: Which attention layers can be replaced by more-efficient layers? How many attention layers can be replaced without sacrificing quality? Which state space layer works best? And what does the trade-off between speed and accuracy look like? In our paper, we compare hybrid models that use three different types of state space models (Gated KalmaNet, Gated DeltaNet, and Mamba-2). Some of our findings: Not all state space models are equal. Under controlled conditions, Gated KalmaNet (GKA) performs best, followed by Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and then Mamba-2. GKA uniquely offers variable-length inference computation without retraining and gives the user direct control over its position on the speed-accuracy frontier. A 32-billion-parameter hybrid model reaches each accuracy threshold faster than an equivalently sized Transformer, converging to similar final accuracy in less wall clock time. The dataset is the AIME 2025 math competition benchmark (hard subset). Accuracy at time t is the fraction of rollouts for which a correct final answer has been produced by time t . A good lossy summary of everything beats a perfect recording of the most recent past. State space models consistently outperform sliding-window attention (SWA), even when SWA gets twice the memory budget. Same quality, twice the throughput. A 32-billion-parameter GKA-based hybrid model matches its source Transformer on reasoning benchmarks while decoding up to twice as quickly with 128,000 tokens of context and reaching correct answers in as little as two-thirds of the wall-clock time. To foster further research on hybrid architectures, we have released a zoo of primed hybrid models at the eight-billion-parameter and 32-billion-parameter scales for long-context reasoning and instruction following, together with training code, optimized kernels, and a vLLM-serving plugin under the Apache 2.0 License. The attention mechanism A Transformer’s attention mechanism — which determines how relevant previously seen tokens are to the token currently being processed — relies on three different vectors, which take their names from database design: the query, the key, and the value. For each token, the query captures what that token is “looking for,” the key captures what it “offers,” and the value carries the actual information it will pass along. Relevance is computed by comparing the current token’s query against every other token’s key; the closer the match, the more that token’s value contributes to the output of attention. Each of these vectors is produced by multiplying the token by a learned weight projection matrix. The Transformer outputs one token at a time, and each output token becomes a new input, so the context grows one token at a time as well. To save computation, the Transformer thus stores the key and value projections of each new input in a “KV cache”. Two kinds of memory layers: Eidetic versus fading The attention mechanism gives Transformers what we call eidetic memory : verbatim recall of every past token. The possibility of recalling over an LLM’s entire context window is what made in-context learning, long-document reasoning, and retrieval-augmented generation possible. But it comes at a cost that scales with the number of input tokens. However, not all attention layers do the same job. Some perform long-range retrieval across tens of thousands of tokens. Others operate more locally, tracking the current clause, copying nearby tokens, and the like. The local ones don't need a growing cache: a compact, fixed-size summary of the past — what we call fading memory — suffices. Hybrid models mix both: attention layers (eidetic, growing cache) for the layers that need global recall and state space layers (fading, fixed size) for the rest. The result is a model with a reduced memory footprint that still has access to verbatim recall where it matters. Priming: Knowledge isn't locked to the architecture Exploring hybrids’ design space has been impractical because each hybrid configuration would normally require pretraining from scratch. Priming sidesteps this by reusing the stored knowledge in a pretrained Transformer's weights. Priming is possible because a Transformer is itself a special case of a state space realization . The outputs of both attention and SSM layers can be expressed as the result of multiplying the value sequence by a “mixing” matrix that decides how much each past token contributes to each current token. Attention computes the mixing matrix by multiplying the query and key matrices; an SSM produces a similar output through a recurrent state of fixed dimension that all past information must pass through. Priming takes advantage of this structural similarity: if an SSM with a fixed-dimensional state can produce a mixing matrix close enough to the attention layer's, the query, key, and value projections from the source Transformer can be reused as the SSM's own input projections, with only the SSM-specific parameters needing to be learned. Whether the approximation holds depends on whether the attention layer performs complex, long-range retrievals or simple, local operations. We distinguish between the two using a cheap empirical proxy: replace each layer with an SWA — which preserves only a fraction of the context — and measure the degradation. Layers that tolerate this substitution are natural candidates for SSM conversion: their mixing matrices don’t need to capture long-range relationships, so the state of an SSM can faithfully represent what they do. This proxy connects to a formal quantity from dynamical-systems theory, the Hankel rank of the layer's mixing matrix , which measures how much information must pass through the state bottleneck and therefore the minimum SSM state dimension required to realize the layer exactly. Priming proceeds in three stages: Layer selection: identify which layers can be faithfully compressed into a fixed-size state while retaining the rest as attention; Weight transfer and alignment: initialize SSM layers from the corresponding attention weights, then run a short distillation process aligning each SSM to the behavior of the layer it replaces; End-to-end adaptation: fine-tune the full hybrid model on next-token prediction, letting all layers coadapt. Priming begins with the use of a simple proxy (a sliding-window attention) to identify attention layers that largely operate locally. The weights of those layers are distilled into state-space-model (SSM) layers, which are then aligned with the behaviors of the layers they replace. Finally, the full hybrid model is fine-tuned on next-token prediction. The entire pipeline consumes less than 0.5% of the source model's pretraining token budget, and it works across Transformer families (Qwen, Llama, Mistral), model classes (dense or MoE), and scales (eight billion to 32 billion and more). With priming we can now explore the design space, the layer type, the hybrid ratio, and layer placement cheaply and systematically, because every variant starts from the same strong initialization and requires minimal training, compared to pretraining. A controlled comparison of fading-memory layers For instance, consider this question: given the same data, the same training budget, and the same ratio of eidetic to fading layers, which SSM layer works best in a hybrid model? In our paper , we evaluate three families of state space models, each representing a different approach to using a fixed-size state: Mamba-2 applies a uniform scalar decay to the entire state at each step, a running average that forgets everything at the same rate. When a new token arrives, it is written into the state, while all previous entries are uniformly attenuated. Mamba-2 is simple and efficient but indiscriminate. Gated DeltaNet (GDN) adds targeted updates on top of uniform decay. Rather than decaying everything uniformly, it can selectively erase the value previously associated with a specific key before writing the new one (the delta rule). This makes it more expressive than Mamba-2: it can revise a specific association without uniformly decaying the rest. Gated KalmaNet (GKA) goes further. Its erase direction depends not only on the current key but on statistics of all past keys , a history-aware update that accounts for the cumulative structure of everything the model has seen. The results of hybrid models using Mamba-2, GDN, and GKA state space models on four tasks. GKA generally outperforms GDN, which always outperforms Mamba-2, in line with theoretical predictions. The theoretical expressiveness hierarchy predicts the empirical one: GKA > GDN > Mamba-2. The gap widens on long-context reasoning, where compression quality matters most, and narrows on short-context tasks. Furthermore, at the 32-billion-parameter (32B) scale, hybrid GKA is within 1% of its source Transformer trained on the same data, despite requiring half the KV cache at inference. Fading memory beats verbatim windowed memory An interesting finding in our study comes from a direct comparison of hybrid models using SSM layers and those using sliding-window attention (SWA), which retain a fixed window of recent tokens verbatim rather than compressing the past into a state. One might expect that verbatim recall, even over a limited window, would outperform lossy compression. After all, no information is lost within the sliding window’s range. And stacking multiple SWA layers increases the “receptive field” of the end-to-end model. Instead, every SSM-based hybrid we tested outperformed the corresponding SWA hybrid on long-context benchmarks, even when the window gets two to four times as much memory as the state. Hybrid models using lossy context summaries (orange) consistently outperformed hybrid models using sliding context windows (teal) . A runtime knob for speed versus accuracy: Variable computation at inference time GKA has a property that neither Mamba-2 nor GDN offers: variable test-time computation. Mamba-2 and GDN have the same computation budget for every input token, regardless of its content. GKA, by contrast, solves a regression problem iteratively, and the iteration count is adjustable at serving time without retraining. The Gated KalmaNet (GKA) accuracy-speed frontier, at four different context lengths. Geometric shapes indicate different numbers of iterations on a regression problem. In practice, serving GKA at 10 iterations instead of its usual 30 sacrifices roughly 1% of its accuracy on AIME 2025 while delivering 10% faster decoding. A single trained model can serve multiple points on the speed-accuracy frontier, so model providers can offer different latency tiers without maintaining separate model variants. This connects to a principle we have discussed in earlier work: intelligence is the ability to allocate effort commensurate with difficulty . GKA's variable-computation mechanism is an architectural embodiment of this principle: a deployment that demands speed can run fewer iterations, while one that demands accuracy can run more. Faster reasoning, not just faster tokens Raw per-token throughput tells only part of the story. A model that is cheaper per token can still be slower end to end if its reasoning is weaker and it needs more tokens to compensate. The deployment-relevant question is how much more rapidly, in wall clock terms, the hybrid reaches a target accuracy. We measured this on AIME 2025, a challenging math competition benchmark, comparing our GKA-Primed-HQwen3-32B-Reasoner against the source Qwen3-32B trained on the same reasoning recipe. Both models generate similar-length thinking traces (a median of about 14,000 tokens on the full set, 28,000 on the hardest problems) — that is, they produce equally in-depth responses — but the hybrid has a much higher throughput. At realistic concurrency levels, where the Transformer's KV cache saturates GPU memory, the hybrid reaches target accuracy thresholds 1.2 to 1.4 times as quickly on the full benchmark and up to 1.6 times as quickly on the hardest problems. This is a consequence of the SSM layers' fixed-size state, which roughly halves the per-sequence memory footprint, enabling more concurrent operations on the same hardware. Decode throughput speedup of GKA-Primed-HQwen3-32B over the source Transformer as a function of context length. Replacing half the attention layers with a fixed-size SSM state roughly halves the size of the KV cache, yielding up to 2.06 times the throughput at a context length of 128,000 tokens. Lowering the number of GKA solver iterations from 30 to 10 at serving time (no retraining necessary) trades a small accuracy margin for additional throughput. The throughput advantage grows with context length: 1.50× at 16K tokens, scaling to 2.06× at 128K for the 32B model (GKA at 10 iterations). With the 8B parameter models, the gains are even greater: 1.94× at 16K to 2.29× at 128K. At long context, KV cache reads dominate the forward pass through the Transformer, and halving the cache roughly doubles the effective batch size at memory saturation. This has implications beyond inference serving. In reinforcement learning (RL) post-training pipelines, throughput gates how rapidly the policy generates correct trajectories. The hybrid's advantage translates directly to a 20% to 100% increase in RL training data rate at a fixed GPU budget. Reasoning accuracy of GKA-primed hybrid models versus source Qwen3 Transformer models across five benchmarks at eight-billion-parameter and 32-billion-parameter scale. Primed hybrid models match their source Transformers in quality at half the memory, and they decode faster. At eight billion parameters, the GKA hybrid uniformly outperforms its GDN counterpart, consistent with the theoretical expressiveness hierarchy GKA > GDN. Beyond the training window: Context extension with state composition Our primed hybrids natively support 128,000 tokens. But agent sessions, codebases, and long legal documents routinely exceed that. Extending context further would normally require another round of continued pretraining on curated data. Can the hybrid architecture itself generalize to longer contexts without additional training ? Existing training-free methods for expanding the context window fall into two classes: those for pure Transformers (positional-embedding rescaling schemes like YaRN) and those for pure SSMs, such as our PICASO , which we presented last year at the International Conference on Learning Representations ( ICLR ). Neither addresses the hybrid setting, where KV caches and recurrent states must be reconciled jointly. In our new arXiv paper , we describe a method of extending hybrid models’ context beyond their native limits without training. The procedure is simple: partition a long input into chunks shorter than the native context length and prepend a shared prefix to each chunk; process all chunks independently in parallel; concatenate the KV caches across chunks while merging the SSM states via the weighted-averaging scheme we introduced in our PICASO paper . State composition for hybrid models. Long inputs are partitioned into chunks at the native context length and processed independently. KV caches are concatenated, while SSM states are merged via the weighted-averaging scheme we proposed in our PICASO paper . This approach enables us to extend the context length of our primed hybrid models from 128K to 256K tokens while preserving substantial accuracy on both retrieval (RULER NIAH) and reasoning (BABILong) tasks at lengths the model was never trained on. In our experiments we show that hybrid state composition preserves the SSM expressivity hierarchy (GKA > GDN > Mamba-2). The hybrid design space is now open All artifacts discussed in this blog are released under the Apache 2.0 License in our Hybrid Model Factory on GitHub and our model zoo on HuggingFace: A collection of primed hybrids for long-context reasoning and instruction following (8B and 32B); The priming training code; Point-to-point sequence parallelism algorithms for SSM layers (up to 2.3 times as fast as all-to-all-based alternatives at multinode scale); Universal sequence parallelism for prototyping novel layers on long sequences without custom kernels or distributed-training expertise; Optimized Triton kernels for GKA decoding and training; A vLLM serving plugin supporting primed hybrid architectures with continuous batching, chunked prefill, and tensor parallelism for inference deployment at scale. If you serve long-context workloads, the 32B GKA reasoning model with the vLLM plugin gives you higher throughput with no quality loss on long context reasoning tasks. If you're scaling RL post-training, the hybrid's throughput advantage means more correct rollouts per unit time at a fixed GPU budget, for faster policy iteration without changing your training recipe. If you're researching new architectures, priming lets you evaluate any layer type under controlled conditions at a fraction of the pretraining cost while starting from a strong initialization. The universal SP module means you don't need custom distributed kernels to train at long context. Priming is not tied to a specific Transformer family or model class. Extending it to Llama, Mistral, or MoE models requires no algorithmic changes. We hope these tools enable the community to explore architectures beyond what we've tested and to develop new algorithms and training recipes for building scalable next-generation architectures for AI agents. For full details, see our paper, " Priming: Hybrid state space models from pre-trained Transformers ". Code, models, and serving plugin are available on GitHub , and the models are also on Hugging Face . Research areas Machine learning Tags Network architectures Agentic AI About the Author Luca Zancato Luca Zancato is a senior applied scientist in Amazon Web Services' Fundamental Research organization.

blogs.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
blogs.author: Anthropic
blogs.description: As our merges per day grew more than tenfold, source control became our biggest development bottleneck. Here, we share how we migrated to an in-house version control system in five months.
blogs.content: At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce. Changes merged to our monorepo per day, from January to September 2026. In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how we were able to quickly build a high-quality, scalable system to deal with it. Growing our monorepo Before we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. While we don’t expect many organizations to have these problems in the very near term, we suspect it won’t be too long before others who use AI coding tools experience these same pressure points, which is why we wanted to share what we built and what we learned. Git is a decentralized system: every clone is a complete, self-contained repository that can compute diffs, read history and blame, and check out any revision while fully offline. For the vast majority of repositories, this is the right design, and it’s a large part of why git became the standard. As our monorepo grows, it increasingly doesn’t fit that design space. The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. Git offers tools for working with a slice of a repository, such as shallow clones, sparse checkouts, and promisor remotes. Beyond these, there are standard workarounds for large monorepos, like internal git mirrors and repository snapshots (seeds) kept in blob storage. We’ve used all of them—at our peak, we operated several hundred internal git mirrors to deal with the load. This bought us time, but they became harder to operate as our merge rate increased. Seeds fell further from the tip of main between refreshes, and it took more and more care to keep operations that depend on history, like diff and blame, working on partial clones. The typical setup for scaling git checkouts. Taking a step back, we noticed that, like most companies, we were using git as a centralized system with one authoritative copy, but nearly all of our clients were agents and jobs that are online by definition. The properties that make git excellent for distributed, offline work were actively undermining our ability to scale as the repo grew. So we asked ourselves: if we designed source control with the fact that agents are always online in mind from the start, what would it look like? Principles for agent-scale source control With agentic coding, many common assumptions about how software is developed are evolving. We embraced these changes when building Scion, which allowed us to take a fundamentally different approach than git on several core principles. Source control for huge monorepos has prior art, notably Google’s Piper and Meta’s Sapling , so we were able to build Scion with their hard-won lessons in mind. Our principles are: Clients are always online. Git assumes that clients work offline and need a complete copy of the repository. Since nearly all of our clients are agents and jobs, we designed Scion’s client and protocols around a server that is always reachable, and have clients fetch data when they need it. Client-server asymmetry. In git, every client is capable of being a full-fledged server. In Scion, the server answers questions about file history and blame, creates commits, performs merges and rebases, and so on. The client maintains a bounded local object cache, lays out the working copy files on disk, monitors for filesystem changes, and gives users an ergonomic way to work with the server. It can compute very little on its own but, in exchange, it requires much less data locally. A comprehensive source control service can power many novel applications. With git, a CI job or tool that needs to ask a question about the repository, such as who last changed a line or how two commits are related, has to maintain a local copy of the repo or hope that vendor-specific APIs provide the answer. With Scion, all of the source control queries the client uses are also exposed via API, so in many cases jobs don’t need a local repository at all. Many internal tools, such as our automated bisect and revert pipelines, wouldn’t be practical at scale without this cheap, programmatic access to source control. Everything must be horizontally scalable. At our peak, we ran several hundred git mirrors, which significantly strained capacity and no longer scaled once the repo outgrew the mirrors’ disks or memory limits. In Scion, the repository’s data is distributed, and every component is independently scalable; there is no fully materialized copy of the repo anywhere, even on the server. There is no equivalent of packfiles (git’s compressed bundles of objects), so no repository maintenance is needed. Commits must be cheap, incremental, and lock-free. In git, you commit locally and then push to share your work. In Scion, every commit, rebase, or merge happens on the server, so there’s nothing to push, but each of those operations needs to be fast. The cost of creating a commit and updating its downstream data structures has to scale with the size of the change, not the overall size of the repo, or the server can’t keep up. The development lifecycle in Scion discourages refs (pointers to commits, such as branches and tags), except for the main ref or release branches, because global state that every server has to agree on is a looming scaling problem. The working copy is optional, and sparse by design. Because our monorepo is so large, and because we check out code tens of millions of times a day for CI, we wanted to avoid checkouts whenever we could. With Scion, a CI job that needs the diff between a commit and its merge base, for example, can ask the server for it. The same goes for writes: many write workloads can also skip the checkout and function entirely via API. Scion’s protocol is centered around sparse checkouts, which only contain the directories the client asks for, and virtualized checkouts, which materialize files on demand, so when a job does need files on disk, the client only pays for what it actually reads. How Scion works It’s helpful to understand how these principles came together in practice when building Scion. These insights can apply to other source control systems or, more broadly, to other stages of the software development lifecycle. Data structures In Scion, the unit of work is a “changeset,” an entry in a write-ahead log. A changeset stores most of what you’d expect from a commit in git. But where a git commit stores a pointer to the tree, a changeset stores a list of the files that changed relative to its first parent, 1 along with content-addressed pointers to the compressed file contents in blob storage. Changesets are created server-side and are available everywhere, instantly. The shape of a changeset in Scion. This structure lets us accept changesets with very high throughput because there are no packfiles to accept, no locking or cross-server coordination, and no refs to move around. Scion does technically support refs, but since neither creating nor fetching commits involves them, moving one is a compare-and-swap on a single Spanner row that happens separately from creating changesets. A changeset records only what’s changed, so on its own, it can’t quickly answer questions like who last edited a line or which commits affected a file. To answer those, Scion builds additional data structures from the changesets, including dedicated structures for file blame and path history and skip lists for the commit graph. We call everything that isn’t directly part of the changeset “derived data,” and we compute it all through one generic mechanism. Each type of derived data is defined recursively, so its value for a changeset is computed from its values for that changeset’s parents. This mechanism has three benefits. First, we can easily add a new type of derived data when a new data structure would make some operation faster. Second, for each type, we can choose whether to compute it eagerly or defer the work, so we avoid materializing data we don’t need. And third, because the client never sees the internals of these data structures, we can optimize them without changing the client. We’ve added new types of derived data many times as the system has grown, such as new indices for performing copy detection or path-based file search. Scaling Scion A small fleet of Scion servers provides source control APIs for any operation a client needs, such as getting changesets, computing diffs, finding merge bases, and fetching blobs. All source control data is content-addressed, so a piece of data never changes once it’s stored, and any server can cache it without checking with the others. As a result, the servers are horizontally scalable and require little coordination. They are essentially large caches that can also compute derived data on the fly and write the results back to Spanner. Scion’s many consumers no longer need to maintain local repositories of their own. Fetching and maintaining the repository used to be a significant maintenance burden for CI jobs or tools that needed to ask source control questions, particularly about commit ancestry and blame. Early in the migration, before we had our own client, repo format, or protocols, Scion only answered these “metadata” queries. Fetching file contents and materializing working copies are far more data-intensive operations, and they needed a design of their own. Scion’s scn client deviates from git’s fetch protocols in several important ways and, as a result, lends itself to a highly scalable architecture that requires significantly less CPU than git servers. Scion’s negotiation doesn’t tell the server what the client already has; instead, it operates exclusively on trees and blobs the client wants. Starting from a root tree, the client checks its local store for missing trees and requests them recursively, then repeats the process for blobs. Every request is for a specific object that never changes, so any cache can answer it, and the architecture closely resembles traditional tiered caches. The process is also efficient and resumable, because there is no single multi-gigabyte packfile response. Sparse and even virtualized checkouts don’t need special support, because the client simply doesn’t ask for trees it doesn’t want. In the fleet, the client talks over a socket to a daemon, scion-daemon, that stores objects for the whole node. Most of our nodes need access to the monorepo, and jobs on the same node reuse most of the same objects. Each daemon starts from a periodically refreshed snapshot, then talks only to the tree and blob cache servers in its region, called scion-cache. These cache servers stream objects directly from memory, in the disk format that the daemon will consume, so they don’t need to spend time computing the client’s missing objects or performing delta compression. When a cache is missing an object, it asks the authoritative scion-servers, which read from Spanner or cloud storage as needed. The scion-daemon, scion-cache, and scion-server all respond to identical RPCs for this protocol, so the client doesn’t need to know the cache topology. Any tier could theoretically talk to any other, but we strictly enforce the tiering to isolate failure domains. We want to avoid a situation where a failure in a regional scion-cache overwhelms the upstream scion-servers and brings down the entire system. Scion’s checkout architecture. Each tier of this system maintains a cache hit rate of over 99% and does not require long-lived state, so it’s easy to scale up if needed. Our Scion infrastructure footprint is now 200x smaller than our previous git mirroring infrastructure in terms of CPU and memory requirements. CI and research jobs check out code two orders of magnitude faster (in seconds rather than minutes), which frees up a sizable amount of capacity across the fleet; CI alone realized a 25% CPU capacity win. Neither clients nor caches need to perform repository maintenance, which simplifies the lifecycle management of our jobs. What we learned building Scion We started building Scion around the same time as Claude Mythos Preview and Claude Tag became available internally. Both of these releases simultaneously amplified the need for Scion and meaningfully accelerated how quickly we could build it. Here’s a particularly striking example. Earlier in the year, we had largely handwritten the first version of the git-to-Scion ingestion pipeline as a prototype. We thought it was good—until we got our hands on an early internal snapshot of Claude Mythos Preview. We asked it to rewrite the whole thing, and with no further instructions, it produced a version that consumed 20x less memory and was 4x faster, while preserving all of the implicit invariants around ingestion ordering and data structures. Merged changes to the Scion and Antique codebases per week, from January to September 2026. What we learned building and operating Scion offers some interesting lessons for what building agent-scale software could look like. Rapid development with a small team will become more common. A team of seven people built both Scion and Antique (our code review tool, which we could easily write a whole other blog post about), not to mention half a dozen related systems, and fully migrated to them in five months. We did all this while the volume of code merged per day increased by 10x. In the past, developing and deploying a source control system like this would have taken a company years of iterative migration, with many more engineers. We think this sort of fast, nimble migration will become more common in the future. Engineers are no less valuable, but their work is changing. All of the engineers who worked on this system would now rate Claude as better at writing code than them. But our engineers still supplied the invaluable understanding of the high-level inter-system components and the design-level tradeoffs, making informed choices around the problems we wanted to solve and the scale we knew we needed to achieve. Very often, we found that the role of the engineers was to tell Claude “no.” Agents will sometimes violate core system constraints to satisfy a pattern that should never have been allowed in the first place. This was particularly common in our migration. For example, there were multiple systems that tried to brute force looking up when a change merged to main by linearly reading the commit log instead of asking our code review tool. Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns. For example, one such review was overly defensive about trusting another internal service, which resulted in Claude adding excessive validation and complexity. Our team members still review every change request for the system, but they now examine the intent of the change as opposed to reading every line of code. We were able to substantially improve optimization and quality. By virtue of Claude’s ability to write immense amounts of code much faster than we could ourselves, Scion is among the most well-tested and well-defended codebases we have ever worked on. Even on our tight timeline, we were able to build hermetic simulations of every non-trivial infrastructure and source control interaction we’ve ever encountered, as well as fuzzing and sophisticated rate limiting. Claude also casually found significant optimizations—for example, an algorithmic optimization to ancestry queries that missed one of our indexes—that would have taken an expert days or weeks of analysis and tuning… and then did it all again the next day. Observed performance improvements on native Scion repos. We laid the groundwork for new forms of monorepo security. Managing safety, security, and compliance in a massive monorepo is as important as managing the size and scale. We built Scion with these in mind from the start. It supports rich access control on repositories, as well as the ability to apply permissions to individual directories in order to protect the most sensitive code without losing the benefits of a monorepo. Furthermore, the code review tooling we built can express complex semantic constraints on approvals, which lets us differentiate simple things like comment-only changes from sensitive logical changes, so that human reviewers can focus on the most consequential changes. A new level of operational excellence is possible. Our team uses Claude Tag heavily, which has helped us monitor each component of the system. For example, we created Slack channels where we tasked Claude with being obsessively focused on the health of a single component. We call these Claudes “superfans.” We have a scion-daemon superfan, a scion-cache superfan, an Antique merge queue superfan, and so on. They have access to our telemetry and logs, and act like an experienced engineer who has nothing better to do than to refresh charts and look for anything strange. We also have traditional alerts for all of our systems, but our superfans can detect subtle and novel issues that make these alerts seem one-dimensional by comparison. We’re completely rethinking our priors. This project prompted us to take a very hard look at other workflows designed for human scale. A proper merge queue, for example, doesn’t make much sense at agent scale. What does CI even mean when hundreds or even thousands of changes can merge while tests are running? We haven’t been able to effectively replicate the industry standard of a global repository lock on the merge queue, so instead, we’ve invested in post-merge and pre-deploy automated testing. This does mean that concurrent changes can conflict, but Claude can typically fix these conflicts faster than humans can even identify them. Contributing to the wider ecosystem We see Scion as just one part of the answer to the scaling concerns that increasingly capable AI agents have raised. We’re sharing these details as an example of how teams can tackle similar challenges, though we don’t expect our solution, or our considerations, to suit every case. Scion is by no means a suitable replacement for git for general use. The concepts we’ve outlined here really only make sense for truly enormous monorepos, with either tens of thousands of engineers or swarms of agents prolifically writing code. Plus, Anthropic is unique in that our ability to spend tokens for internal use far exceeds what any other business would realistically want to spend. We do this both to address our own software development needs, and to test Claude’s capabilities. Practically speaking, it’s difficult to offer Scion in a form that would be broadly useful to other organizations. It diverges significantly from git, meaning companies would need to migrate every piece of the development lifecycle, and it requires its own code review, code search, and CI. Our internal versions of these components are highly bespoke, so they would be difficult for other organizations to adopt, and we worry that attempting to build a public version that tries to please everyone wouldn’t actually be very useful. However, we anticipate that this class of problems will become more commonplace over the next six to 12 months, and it would be an inefficient use of engineering resources for every company using git to face similar challenges alone. Given that, we think the most impactful thing we can do is to share our thinking, so that other developers can apply some of the most successful parts of Scion to git without departing from the overall model. A git server doesn’t have to work the same way as a git client does; novel server architectures exist that provide significant scaling improvements. Git platforms can provide comprehensive server-side RPCs like Scion, perhaps even in a standardized way across forges that the git client can learn to talk to. The negotiation protocol doesn’t have to look exactly like it does today, either, and the various sparse and shallow features in git can be made to compose well. Lastly, we want to acknowledge that the git community has spent nearly two decades scaling the platform for millions of developers. Our contribution is far narrower: sharing our early view into how agentic software development interacts with these systems, so that we can partner with GitHub, GitLab, and the OSS community to support the changing needs of developers. We’re all in it together as the software development lifecycle intersects with the AI exponential. Acknowledgements Written by Nick G. and the source control team: S.G., R.K., Dan C., Garrett H., Ben L., Colin M., Joe P. We’re grateful to Vilas J. and Sergiu D. for supporting the source control team on this ambitious journey and Amir O. for early contributions to Antique. Footnotes Storing changed files relative to the first parent of a merge is a stylistic choice; in practice, we’ve found that people only care about history or blame for commits on the main line in trunk-based development in a monorepo.

Two remedies exist: aggressive hyperparameter tuning such as high weight decay, and mixing in data from a high-resource auxiliary language to directly aid the low-resource target. While hyperparameter tuning regularizes the model by shrinking weights to restrict network capacity, auxiliary data mixing uses a tunable mixing ratio to expand the training distribution and diversify the training signal with new knowledge. Both offer a principled way to improve training in a data-constrained domain. We compare these levers systematically across four model scales from 150M to 1.43B parameters, using Arabic as the low-resource target and English as the auxiliary, over approximately 1000 pre-training runs. Three findings emerge. First, mixing yields larger improvements than hyperparameter tuning on both validation loss and downstream task accuracy, and the gap grows with model size. Mixing regularizes by diversifying the training signal and contributes knowledge the repeated target corpus cannot supply; validation loss captures only the first effect. blogs.content: research area Speech and Natural Language Processing conference EMNLP content type paper published October 2026 Large Language Models for Machine Translation Quality Annotation: Humans and Models Are Both Challenged Authors Hala Almaghout, Christian Federmann, Qin Gao View publication Copy Bibtex Large Language Models (LLMs) are considered to be a more efficient and cost-effective alternative to human judgment for Machine Translation (MT) evaluation. With MT evaluation spanning a large number of language pairs, domains and levels of annotation granularity, LLMs must be thoroughly evaluated across these dimensions before being reliably used as alternatives to human evaluation. In this paper, we evaluate the performance of LLMs for two prominent MT quality evaluation schemes: Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM) and Error Span Annotation (ESA) by comparing their agreement with human annotators. We present results on a long-context test set of 70 language pairs and the publicly available WMT23 and WMT25 data, investigating both score and error span annotation agreement across a variety of language pairs and domains. Our results show that while LLM agreement with human annotators exceeds agreement between human annotators for some evaluation tasks, both vary substantially across annotation schemes, language pairs and domains and remain unreliable for most settings. Furthermore, we identify challenges facing both human and LLM annotators: humans are particularly challenged by fine-grained MQM annotations and low-resource language pairs, while LLMs struggle with minor errors, wrong language variants and error span annotation. Our results highlight the potential for improvement for both human and LLM annotation performance, possibly through human-LLM collaborative annotation pipelines that address the reliability issues identified in this work. At the same time, modern Apple Silicon–based macOS devices are equipped with powerful GPUs that remain largely idle during normal usage. This paper presents Minions, a dynamic and distributed virtual GPU cloud that aggregates idle Apple Silicon GPUs across macOS devices to execute large-scale machine learning inference workloads. Minions enables teams to leverage existing hardware without requiring additional GPU procurement. The system provides flexible GPU inference task execution, fault tolerance, and efficient resource utilization. Our experience shows that idle macOS devices can be transformed into a practical distributed GPU inference platform in environments where centralized GPU resources are constrained. blogs.content: 0:00 / 0:00 Gemini 4 Argon in Google Antigravity The Antigravity Team · Oct 13, 2026 · 6 min read Share Copy link Share on X Share on Bluesky Share on LinkedIn Since the beginning, we built Google Antigravity for an agent-first future, designing foundational primitives that would scale alongside model intelligence. With Gemini 4 Argon, the agent-first experience truly comes to life in the Antigravity app. Earlier this month, we introduced Gemini 4 Argon, our latest model with frontier performance in complex workflows across real-world software engineering, enterprise knowledge work like legal and finance, and cybersecurity defense. Today, we’re rolling out Gemini 4 Argon directly inside Google Antigravity for Google AI Ultra subscribers — available in the Antigravity desktop app and the Antigravity CLI. For businesses , Gemini 4 Argon is available via the API in Gemini platform and within Antigravity on eligible Gemini Enterprise subscriptions. While Argon is designed to tackle your hardest problems, we’re equally excited about future models that can be used as everyday drivers for an even broader range of builders. Accelerating development across Google Our most honest proving ground is our engineering teams. Before bringing Argon to developers in Antigravity, we put it to work inside Google. Today, over 100K users across Alphabet rely on Argon inside our internal version of Antigravity each month to solve complex production problems across our codebases. Over a four-week period, we have seen a 35% increase in agentic code, improving not just developer velocity, but code quality with a 30% decrease in post-submit rollbacks. Here are a few ways teams across Alphabet have been putting Argon in Antigravity to work on our hardest engineering challenges in products you love: YouTube comment optimization: Argon in Antigravity helped the team cut the CPU footprint of YouTube’s comments frontend in half. By tracing production profile data, Argon identified that redundant emoji rendering alone accounted for nearly 45% of server overhead, leading to 12 targeted optimizations. The updates reduced server comment-load latency by 30 ms and dropped client end-to-end latency by 20 ms. Debugging Wing drone physics simulator: Argon in Antigravity reviewed Wing’s proprietary internal drone physics simulator, reasoning through the underlying physics and math rather than just the structure of the code. It highlighted areas for improved physics simulations and proposed 18 targeted modelling improvements across aerodynamics, propulsion, and structural dynamics to resolve long-standing legacy issues. Operating at Google-scale forced us to build Antigravity to be enterprise-ready from Day 1, transforming our day-to-day development across Google. By streamlining routine tasks that every enterprise development team faces, from refactoring legacy codebases to automating test coverage and resolving build breakages, Argon is freeing engineers to focus on higher-level architecture and product innovation: Burning down the backlog: Argon in Antigravity took an aging queue of 134 open bug reports spanning multiple services, and ran agents to work out which were still real, cross-referencing commit histories, checking whether candidate fixes actually reached production, and inspecting live telemetry for whether the error still occurs. In under 3 hours it closed 97 stale or duplicate bugs with documented commit proof (a 72.4% queue reduction) and sorted the remaining 37 by owner with no unassigned tickets left. Migrating legacy code: For decades, vital scientific research has been locked inside fragile legacy codebases like Fortran. Using a custom skill within Antigravity, a team deployed Argon to map and execute a complete rewrite into modern Rust. Argon autonomously delivered the modernized codebase, achieving a 1.8x performance boost and memory safety while giving scientists a robust foundation for future work. Performing security audits: Argon in Antigravity was used to audit a batch of access-control changes. Argon traced how permissions actually flowed at runtime rather than just reading the code diff, and found four critical security bugs. Two earlier frontier models had audited the identical code and both concluded there were zero security holes. Triaging production support tickets: Argon in Antigravity batch-processes dozens of tickets from an on-call rotation. It sorts them by issue type, tracing root causes through the code and logs, proposing fixes and drafting the replies for human approval. This has freed up 2-3 hours per shift, enabling the team to focus on resolving issues faster. We are excited to provide our Gemini for business customers the same day-to-day acceleration that we’ve been seeing with Antigravity. Argon across disciplines One of the most encouraging things we’ve observed internally is how quickly teams outside core software engineering have adapted Argon in Antigravity for their own use cases. Monthly active usage outside of core engineering is soaring, with over half of Cloud sales, almost half of finance, and over a third of business and operations Googlers using Antigravity. Plugins, skills, and MCP integrations make it straightforward to connect the agent to specialized data sources and workflows. Using these customizations with Argon makes it easier to integrate with deep verticalized work, such as: Marketing website localization: The Antigravity DevRel team used Argon in Antigravity to localize hundreds of pages of developer documentation into 17 languages in a matter of hours. This improved the accessibility and UX of the website by shrinking a multi-week process down to hours and shifting human effort exclusively to high-quality review. Resolving a data dashboard outage: A TPM (Technical Program Manager) used Argon in Antigravity to autonomously resolve a critical P0 data center dashboard outage that had stalled for over four months. Without needing dedicated engineering support, the TPM diagnosed deep cross-stack database failures and landed a 3,200-line pipeline overhaul, restoring real-time visibility in just a few days. Vetting sales prospects: Argon in Antigravity built an automated qualification workflow for an account executive in Ads sales that checks prospective company website traffic, confirms the site has clear conversion funnels, and cross-references the sales database to see whether the account is a qualified prospect. This reduced research time by 90%, saving the account executive upwards of 10 hours of manual work each week so they can spend time on direct client outreach instead. Financial planning and analysis: With custom finance plugins, a finance lead used Argon in Antigravity for end-to-end financial reconciliations, budget tracking, contract extraction, and daily executive briefings across 80 separate workflows. Over seven business days, 15.5 hours of human direction produced about 335 human-equivalent hours of validated financial output, saving more than eight weeks of manual work. Getting started Argon is rolling out starting today in the Google Antigravity desktop app and CLI for Google AI Ultra subscribers , eligible Gemini Enterprise subscriptions , and in the API in Gemini platform. Update to the latest version of Antigravity to try it on your most complex workflows. We’d love to hear what you build and where we can make the experience better. blogs.title: Preparing chip designers for the nanostack era
blogs.author: Peter Hess
blogs.description: IBM is releasing a process design kit for our groundbreaking 0.7-nanometer transistor architecture.
blogs.content: Earlier this year, IBM announced the world’s first 0.7nm node chip technology . Built on a totally redesigned transistor architecture that layers nanosheets on top of each other, the nanostack overcomes the spatial limitations of packing more transistors into a given footprint. In short, it unlocks the Z axis to reimagine logic scaling for the modern era. The result is nearly 100 billion transistors on a 150mm 2 chip, almost double the density of IBM’s 2nm node chip , with 50% better performance and 70% more energy efficiency, as well as 40% scaling in SRAM memory. Now, as the semiconductor industry approaches this major transition in transistor architecture, IBM is announcing plans to make available an early research and development process design kit, or PDK, for the 7-angstrom nanostack technology in the first quarter of 2027. As the industry stands on the verge of this new era in semiconductor design, the PDK is intended to give organizations an early opportunity to explore how this emerging architecture can change their offerings. A PDK provides the models, design rules, libraries, and other information engineers need to begin designing chips for a particular manufacturing process. IBM’s planned offering will help semiconductor companies evaluate nanostack technology well before it is ready for widespread adoption. Potential collaborators include fabless chip companies, electronic design automation (EDA) vendors, equipment suppliers, and research organizations interested in developing the technology. “We want to invite people to work with us on the early PDK evaluation, and then on codifying the technology together,” said Jingyun Zhang, senior technology enablement manager at IBM Research. Preparing for the future, together IBM’s nanostack chip architecture represents a substantial departure from today’s nanosheet transistors. Instead of positioning n-type and p-type devices next to each other, the architecture stacks one above the other. This approach changes the physical layout of a circuit and introduces new considerations for resistance, capacitance, thermal behavior , and interactions between the upper and lower devices. “The biggest difference is in the device structure,” Zhang said. “When people are trying to design a circuit now, they will need to shift their thinking from how things worked in the previous nanosheet generation, because the layout is changing from 2D to 3D at transistor level for the first time in logic foundry technology.” The first version of the PDK is expected to include exemplary standard-cell libraries for logic functions and an exemplary SRAM design. Circuit designers will be able to use these resources to investigate placement and routing, produce early block-level layouts, and evaluate potential density and power-performance characteristics. The initial release will not contain every model that a mature commercial PDK would include. Instead, it will advance collaborative research, establishing for the first time a foundation for design-technology co-optimization in a technology’s early phase on an open hardware innovation platform. What’s next For prospective partners, early access to the nanostack PDK offers more than a preview of a future transistor. It creates an opportunity to investigate how nanostack technology might be optimized for specific products. EDA companies can begin adapting their design tools to the architecture, while equipment makers can study the specialized fabrication challenges associated with its structure. Researchers can also explore areas such as parasitic extraction, thermal coupling, and device-to-device interactions as the technology develops. “The PDK will help people migrate from nanosheet to nanostack,” Zhang said. “We are standing at a point where we can help the industry get better prepared.” Previous shifts — from planar transistors to FinFETs and from FinFETs to nanosheets — required the industry to rethink both fabrication and chip design. By making an early nanostack PDK available, IBM aims to give companies time to begin that process again, this time with an opportunity to help co-define the technology’s design ecosystem from the outset.

blogs.name: IBM Research Blog
blogs.title: Making AI-driven chip design affordable with open agent factories and distributed inference at scale
blogs.author: Peter Hess
blogs.description: Open frontier models and llm-d enabled IBM Research to explore quantum error correction hardware at 11.5× lower inference cost than an all-proprietary configuration.
blogs.content: As AI systems become more capable, researchers are increasingly asking a practical question: Can AI do more than help write code for computing systems? Specifically, can it actively participate in the design of complex computing systems and rapidly translate algorithms into silicon? New work in AI-driven chip design suggests the answer is yes. But a promising algorithm is only the beginning of a hardware design. Turning it into an efficient chip requires exploring how to organize computation, move data, and use limited hardware resources. Each choice opens up alternatives. Each alternative takes engineering effort to implement and evaluate. AI agents can expand that exploration. Working together, they can propose architectural changes, write implementations, check correctness, and use synthesis results to decide what to try next. The obstacle is cost: the LLM tokenomics for hardware design and the cost-efficiency of design space exploration. A single search campaign can consume hundreds of millions of tokens, and applying the approach across many components and design revisions could require hundreds of such campaigns. A new demonstration from IBM Research shows how open frontier models and efficient distributed inference can change the calculation. Using an agent factory to optimize hardware for quantum error correction, researchers achieved a 52-times speedup over the baseline design in high-level synthesis estimates for approximately $26 in inference cost. Under the same search budget, a proprietary frontier model configuration cost 11.5 times more than a configuration using open frontier models throughout — $299 versus $26, respectively. The proprietary configuration achieved higher speedup (204x), but the open-model configuration established a different result: Substantial hardware optimization can be achieved with a much smaller inference budget, along with the smallest area design. That cost advantage creates an opportunity to apply automated exploration more widely, and to reinvest the savings in finding better designs. The results also suggest that the practical value of AI-assisted chip design depends on more than the best design an agent can produce. It also depends on how much verified exploration an organization can afford. Model capability, the assignment of agent roles, and the infrastructure serving those models all shape the hardware improvements that are attainable within a real engineering budget. By combining open frontier models with llm-d’s low-cost distributed inference , IBM has demonstrated that AI agent factories can move beyond coding assistance and become active participants in hardware design, and they can do it affordably. From generating code to exploring architectures Hardware design remains one of the most expertise-intensive activities in computing. High Level Synthesis (HLS) raises the level of abstraction from register-transfer level (RTL), used in hardware design languages, to C or C++, but engineers must still make countless decisions about loop structure, parallelism, memory organization, dataflow, and synthesis directives. Those choices interact in complex ways. For example, performing more calculations simultaneously helps only if the memory system can supply their inputs. A design that runs faster may also require more hardware resources. Finding a useful balance requires repeated experiments, and the design space quickly becomes too large for humans to explore exhaustively. An ‘ agent factory ’ organizes that work. “An agent factory turns hardware optimization into a coordinated cycle of exploration: A coordinator agent directs parallel worker agents to develop and synthesize alternative designs within a defined search budget,” said Ruchir Puri, IBM fellow and IBM Research chief scientist. When these agents are set to their task, they independently explore optimization strategies. “A verifier checks that the proposed improvements are valid, and the designs are ranked by latency and hardware resource use. Those results guide the next round of exploration, allowing the factory to refine its search as it discovers better designs,” added Puri. Rather than searching for a single solution, the factory investigates many possibilities in parallel, using synthesis feedback to guide future exploration. In the new study, the coordinator planned the search and assigned optimization hypotheses to four parallel worker agents. The workers modified the decoder implementation, and correctness checks and HLS results provided feedback for subsequent rounds. Each configuration received a budget of 100 hypotheses. The agents explored changes with architectural consequences. One transformation reorganized message storage so that the synthesis tool could identify independent memory accesses and execute more work in parallel. Another replaced sequential reductions with tree structures that exposed parallel computation. The value came from connecting code changes to their hardware effects through repeated evaluation. A classical hardware challenge at the heart of quantum computing The key question addressed in the new paper was whether this approach can be scaled cost-effectively using open frontier models and distributed inference infrastructure. To evaluate that idea, Puri and his team demonstrated the approach using Relay-BP, a quantum error correction decoding algorithm, for the [[144,12,12]] bivariate bicycle code. Quantum error correction relies on classical computation. Measurements provide clues about errors affecting quantum information, and a decoder must interpret those clues and infer corrections. Doing that quickly, within practical hardware resource limits, is an essential part of building fault-tolerant quantum systems. Relay-BP is a useful test because its repeated message passing is inherently parallel, but the baseline implementation's sparse graph representation and memory-access patterns make that parallelism difficult for HLS tools to exploit. That also makes the decoder a demanding test of AI-driven hardware exploration because the agents must preserve the computation while changing how the hardware performs it. What the same search budget buys The researchers compared three configurations under the same 100-hypothesis budget: a proprietary frontier model as both coordinator and workers, an open frontier model in both roles, and a hybrid with a proprietary coordinator and open-model workers. The open model ran on premises through llm-d. Each configuration explored 100 hypotheses. Costs cover model inference, rather than the full hardware development workflow. All three found verified hardware improvements, but they produced distinct tradeoffs. Open and hybrid searches found useful compact designs, while the proprietary configuration more effectively converted additional resources into parallelism and lower latency. Each configuration was evaluated in one search run, so these results characterize the observed searches rather than establish a universal model ranking. The all-open search also used more tokens: approximately 241 million, compared with 216 million for the all-proprietary search. Its lower cost came from the economics of serving those tokens. This distinction matters for agent factories, where each hypothesis can involve many rounds of reasoning, coding, debugging, and interpreting tool results. Why inference infrastructure matters An agent factory repeatedly returns to much of the same information: source code, design constraints, earlier changes, and synthesis reports. Efficient serving can reuse computation associated with that shared context. The study used llm-d, an open-source distributed inference framework, to support this workload. Its cache-aware routing directs requests toward servers holding reusable context. It also separates prompt processing from token generation, allowing the system to allocate resources to each independently. These capabilities help reduce repeated work and use accelerator capacity efficiently . As enterprises seek to rein in rising inference costs and maintain control of their sensitive data, this latest demonstration showed that open-weight models deployed on-premises through llm-d’s distributed inference stack can dramatically lower serving costs while still discovering valuable hardware optimizations. For the chip-design workload, the paper reports a prefix-cache hit rate of approximately 98% and a blended serving cost of about $0.11 per million tokens. The deployment served the factory alongside other agent workloads on shared infrastructure. Open weights also allowed the team to run the model on premises and retain control over the design artifacts processed by those agents. The cost advantage therefore reflects the combination of an open model and an efficient serving system. Both contribute to making sustained exploration affordable. What’s next: Turning lower cost into better designs Lower inference cost creates room for additional search, but spending more does not automatically produce proportionate improvements. Extending the all-open campaign from 100 to 200 hypotheses increased its speedup from 52× to 60×. The gains continued, but they diminished. The next step is to improve how the agent factory uses that additional budget. Future work will explore adaptive allocation of resources, a wider range of architectural hypotheses, and selective use of stronger models for difficult transformations or search coordination. The aim is to navigate the cost–quality tradeoff deliberately: deciding where additional reasoning, a different model, or a new architectural direction is most likely to improve the design. Evaluation will also need to account for synthesis and verification costs alongside inference. Lowering one part of the workflow is most valuable when the complete process can support the additional exploration it enables. AI for chip design connects two forms of progress into a reciprocal relationship: Better hardware enables more capable AI, and more capable AI can help engineers develop better hardware. Cost-efficient agent factories make that relationship more practical. By making each search more affordable, open models and distributed inference create room to test more ideas and, with better search strategies, turn that opportunity into better chips.
